blocks.text: My Lord, Anna Milan, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR ANNA MILAN (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Thank you. Could we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's Anna Margaret Milan.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. I understand it's Dr Milan?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, but Anna is fine.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I know the temptation is, because I am asking the questions, to direct the answers at me, but if you could keep your voice up please and ensure that it is projected to the back of the court, we would be very grateful.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I apologise, I've had a cold, so if you can't hear me, do shout.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I am sure someone will let us know if there is a problem.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I am a consultant clinical biochemist at Liverpool Royal.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. I think you worked specifically in the clinical biochemistry unit at Liverpool University Foundation NHS Hospital Trust?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You have been asked to comment on a blood sample that arrived at your laboratory, is that right --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- in the name of [Baby F]? [Baby F] was born on 29 July 2015.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And you've had the opportunity to look at the records at the laboratory in that regard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. I think you were able to confirm, were you, that a blood sample taken from [Baby F] was received from the Countess of Chester Hospital at 4.15 in the afternoon of 6 August 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And that that sample was submitted to be tested for insulin and C-peptide levels?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. How are samples delivered, please, to your laboratory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It very much depends on the nature of the test that's required. With insulin and C-peptide they have to be stored frozen, so that would have come via courier or taxi in a bag that is temperature controlled to maintain that sample integrity.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Once the sample arrives, just so we understand -- where precisely is the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've just moved into a new building but it used to be in the Duncan Building as part of the Royal Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: The specimen reception, which is where the bag would have arrived, is on the ground floor and then it's brought up to the fourth floor.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What happens, please, with the sample when it first arrives in its frozen form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If it's a frozen sample it's treated as a priority to make sure that sample stays frozen, so every sample is taken individually with the request form to make sure that the patient name, date of birth and identifier, whether that's NHS or hospital number, match the details on the request form. If that happens then the sample is just refrozen with a bar code number on it.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So on arrival, triage involves checking it has all the necessary detail --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- to identify its origin and the purpose of the sampling?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And then it's placed in your own freezer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Okay. How, once this process of checking and triaging the arrival of the sample is complete and it is placed in the freezer, what happens to the sample next and within what sort of time frame?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again it very much depends on what tests are requested and also if it's stated as urgent. So at that time -- this was obviously 6/7 years ago -- insulin and C-peptides were measured in a batch; by that I mean they are not run in real time. And that's largely because we're an adult hospital, so we don't get urgent requests. So if it had been requested as urgent, we may have put it on the analyser that day, but at that stage this sample wasn't requested as an urgent, so it was frozen until we ran the batch the following week.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So at that time, because of the nature of the bulk of the work that you received, insulin/C-peptide requests would be done together in batches?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And your recollection is that was the following week?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: All right. Now, does the sample have to be defrosted before it is analysed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes. So before we defrost anything, just so again to maintain sample integrity, we make sure all the maintenance is done on that analyser and it passes all of its QC checks. By that I mean that it is fit to run before we defrost any samples.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So in the context of this particular sample and insulin and C-peptide, is a specific machine used for that process?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is. I know it doesn't mean a lot, but it is what we call a standalone machine. So it's in a separate room, so it has somebody dedicated to run it, and once that's -- it's routine, it's a routine analyser, but we have dedicated people to run it and make sure it's fit before anything goes on it.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Again, in the context of insulin and C-peptide, that's a machine that would be gone to with a batch from time to time and before anything was analysed on it, it would be --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- what, the maintenance would be checked?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All maintenance is done and there's various procedures, documented SOPs, as would be expected in a laboratory.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Pausing there, sorry, SOPs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Standard operating procedures. We are under accreditation by a governing body and to make sure our lab is fit for purpose we have to have very documented procedures in place to ensure that everything is standardised, so machines are fit for purpose but are fit for purpose the same as they would be in any laboratory in the UK.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. So you mentioned you're part of a standard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Who sets that standard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's UKAS, UK Laboratory Accreditation Schemes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Do the manufacturers have any input on those maintenance procedures?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They do. So they dictate what maintenance they deem is necessary for that machine to be running. They're very standardised procedures. They have to be ticked before the machine can actually be used.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Would any sample be placed within the machine before all of those maintenance checks were completed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: We've mentioned the manufacturer. Can you confirm who the manufacturer is and whether it's significant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Our manufacturer for all of our analysers is Roche in the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: How would you characterise Roche in your industry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They're global. They are a massive business, UK, US, globally, and one of the largest suppliers of laboratory equipment in the UK and worldwide.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And do they provide the additional equipment to go with the machine that's required for the testing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they provide all of the consumables that are needed, all of the reagents, all of the QC material -- and that's material that, once you have done your maintenance, then you have to test it to make sure it's performing, and all of the calibration standards as well.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You mentioned QC, that stands for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Quality control.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, I talk in abbreviations.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Forgive me for being pedantic.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: The fact that this company, Roche, provide all the equipment, does that give rise to a particular term that you use for the collective?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In the sense of?
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Well, Roche assays. Could you explain what they are?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The term assay is -- so insulin is an assay, Cpeptide is an assay. Everything that we run per analyte is deemed an assay. So overall Roche probably are responsible for about 400 to 500 assays that can be available.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. You mentioned the standards that are maintained.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once the machine has been checked, quality assured, the standard procedures have been run through and the analysis is completed, what happens then with the results?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then we defrost the samples, ensuring they've been defrosted and mixed, and then they are placed on the analyser ready for analysis. They go through, depending on how long and which assay, they might take 20 minutes/half an hour for analysis, and then the results are held. So we always put QC through after as well to ensure that during that time window that machine was performing appropriately. And once those QCs, quality controls, at the end of that batch are analysed and are deemed appropriate, then all the results that were run between those two time points are then released on to a technical validation system.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Can I just break that down a little bit? You told us you do more than one sample on each batch?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So, did I understand this correctly, that the results are held in a holding area almost --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- whilst another quality assessment run is -- takes place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What does that involve, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, that's just running through what we call quality control material. So they have assigned values for each of these analytes and we have a window of which deem them acceptable, so a range by which if it doesn't hit that range, then we'd have to reject that batch and re-run it. So we always put them through at the beginning and the end, particularly on a standalone analyser, which is one that's used in batches, to make sure
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: during that time window everything is running appropriately. So they go through at the beginning and they have to pass before we put samples on. And they go through at the end to determined that during that time window, whether it be 3 hours or 4 hours, that everything was running appropriately.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: It's not until you're satisfied, at the start and the end, of the efficiency of the system that you then release from that holding --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- position? Where do the results go from there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then they go -- that's what we call technical validation. So one of the lab staff will have looked at the results of the QC at the beginning, they'll have looked at the results of those quality controls at the end, and they will then what's called technically validate. And then they come on to a list for a biochemist, which is myself and others, to then review clinically with whatever information we may have been given.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So once everybody is satisfied that the machine is working accurately and that the results as produced are accurate, then they go on to a human analysis, if I can put it that way --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- to consider what the numbers mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Would that be a fair way to put it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Interpretation?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: A much quicker way to put it. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what happens at that stage then, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that stage they are put on what we call a list, just for an easy term. We've got a technical term for it but it goes on to a list. Then, as a biochemist, we get a report that shows us the QC data so we can actually then confirm that technically they'd been validated, which I know is sort of -- makes it another level of checking. Then we start to look at them. If
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: there's been information on the request form we can add an appropriate clinical comment. If the numbers themselves speak, so what they say, we can also add a comment just based on the numbers as well.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Once they've been through the human filter, if I can put it that way, what happens to the results then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Depending on the nature of the comments that we might put on there, if it's something that we require or we deem that needs telephoning to the requester, whether that be an inpatient doctor or whether that's an external hospital, we will then phone that result through to the requesting location, especially back in -- when this was done we still required snail mail, it wasn't as electronically based as it currently is.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So rather than wait for a paper report to get through to the requesting location, if it was deemed appropriate we would have phoned a result through.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: We'll come to that in a moment, but perhaps we should deal with the results of this particular sample next.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The sample was labelled, you checked, as having been taken at 17.56 on 5 August 2015; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: It was analysed within your laboratory and the results for this particular sample were -- and I think in fact you've provided a printout of the results; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: If I can ask Mr Murphy to put AM1 on the screen, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not something we've seen before. This is a document I'm sure you recognise from your professional life.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you just please confirm for us what the results showed as a result of the analysis that you have described to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This screen obviously looks a bit alien because it's what we would see on our in-system -- what we call Telepath, which is how we interpret our results. But just to orientate you, the top left is the unique identifiers, that's the hospital number of the patient.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Obviously at that stage, the name -- because when the request came in it might have been that they were referred to as twin 1,
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: twin 2 without a first name, so we've kept with that with twin 2 on the request form.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Date of birth and the requesting location.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: The specimen number is the unique identifier we'd have given that sample when it came into the laboratory once we had checked all the demographics, so that the name matched with the request form.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Obviously the collected time is the time it was collected at the referral location.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Then underneath you've got 6 August, 16.15. That is when we booked it into the system, so that time is when it was actually booked in.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Underneath you have three tests -- we'll, you've got two tests but two different units for insulin. So C-peptide is reported in picomoles per litre. And the value of less than 169 means it was undetectable on our system, so that's the lower report. We couldn't measure it in our assay.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Sorry, pausing there, there comes a point where there is such a small amount that even your computer can't -- your testing equipment can't detect its presence?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And the threshold for that presumably is 169?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So when it says less than 169, that could be zero, that could be 168 or anywhere in between?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Basically it means that we cannot accurately give it a number because it could be anything below that or it could be completely zero, but the assay itself can't distinguish anything below that number.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then the insulin it reported in two different units.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: But the important one with relation to the C-peptide is the one that's got SI in brackets next to it. That's the international reporting units. That puts it in the same units as the Cpeptide, which is picomoles per litre. So it's only a factor different, it's not that we've measured it twice. There's a multiplication factor involved. But the important one is the
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: 4,657, because that's in the same units as the C-peptide, and obviously they come from the same molecule, so that's what gives you your indication.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So just dealing with that briefly, so I understand it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In order to compare the two figures, please correct me if I'm wrong, they are expressed in exactly the same measurement or by means of the same measurement --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- so that there's no, as it were, distortion between the comparison?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If you're looking for ratios, which is what you tend to look at for interpretation, you're looking at the SI units for insulin and then the C-peptide so you can calculate your ratio of C-peptide to insulin.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You mentioned before that in some circumstances the hospital involved will be called, there's a telephone call takes place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You're able to confirm that happened in this particular case involving [Baby F]. If we can look, please, you provided, I think, a note of the telephone call; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We do try and -- obviously it's not always possible but we do try and keep a complete audit trail end to end so that we can determine who a result was telephoned by.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could go to AM2, please. Can you confirm this is the document you were able to provide?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Please tell us or just explain to us briefly what this tells you, knowing the system that was in place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Again, it's not a particularly attractive screen, but what it documents is the result that we telephoned, which was the C-peptide and insulin, who it was telephoned by, and where to. So it was telephoned to the Countess of Chester biochemist, which would be the equivalent of one of us at Chester, and where it was telephoned and what time. The advice we would have given them would also be the comment that was reported when they got the paper report as well.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And we can see there:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Advice information: low C-peptide to insulin."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Is that, as you were telling us before, how you enter them in the same measurements --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- so that a comparison can be made? Is that what you were alluding to there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You then have:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Question mark] exogenous"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's our shorthand way of putting "query exogenous". So while it might look as though it's a question mark, it's a shorthand we often use for query. So we're just basically saying, "Is this exogenous? It looks like it is".
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Okay. Very briefly, why does that stand out as exogenous?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The C-peptide is undetectable and in health C-peptide should be a lot higher than insulin because it's got a longer half-life and it's not active. So insulin is quickly cleared, so in health your ratio should be between 5 and 10 C-peptides to insulin.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So it should be considerably higher than --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The insulin --
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) not considerably lower?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Suggest send sample to Guildford for exogenous insulin."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just explain that to us please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not a standard comment and it's not something that most people take up. But in a case where there is a suggestion of exogenous insulin, if people wanted to determine the type,
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Guildford is a specialist laboratory that can help. They have assays that can distinguish between the sources of the insulin. By that I mean is it human or -- because obviously some insulin supplements are bovine in origin or porcine, so they can help distinguish between that. But it's not something people tend to take up unless there's a real difficulty in trying to understand where that insulin came from.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. Who is that a decision for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's for the requesting location to discuss with the clinical team.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So it appears, on your note, on the basis -- that that's something that would have been raised with them rather than something you would have been considering --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- from your perspective?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, we wouldn't have sent a sample on unless there was a clinical demand for it. The results speak for themselves, so it's unlikely that it would be sent on.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: By putting that, it implied that we would keep the sample as well if they did want to send it on.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right, okay. And how long would the sample have been kept for whilst that decision was being made?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We would have kept it for at least 7 days because it would have been refrozen after the assay.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You mentioned Guildford and you told us about the type of quality assurance that takes place within your laboratory.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Is there a quality assurance process from outwith the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So every laboratory, as part of the UKAS accreditation, which was the governing body I mentioned earlier, we also have to participate in what's called external quality assessment. And this is a body that sends us anonymised samples every 4 weeks that we have to run through all of our assays as patients and then return the results, so you can see if your assay is performing in line with all the other Roche users in the UK.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So you -- is this right, Guildford presumably is the HQ for your particular area of expertise; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Guildford is -- that's a separate laboratory, it's like our laboratory, but their specialism is insulin/C-peptide. But the external quality assurance is done by a body called Birmingham Quality. They basically cover all of the laboratories in the UK and send out these samples as part of their accreditation scheme. It's another level of checking.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Another level of checking the efficiency of your laboratory, not internally but externally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: That happens on a regular basis?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, on a regular basis. It is retrospective because obviously you have analysed them, the results have been reported, but it helps you try and identify if you've ever got any problems, whether it's a manufacturer-based issue, so if everybody performs badly, or whether it's an individual laboratory performance.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Were there any problems at any time around the time of this sample in --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Does that enable you to express any view as to the confidence you have in the results you have just explained to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very confident in the results. I mean, the pattern is very clear-cut. It's not numbers that -- obviously the C-peptide is below the limit of quantification --
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- but the insulin is very much in the measuring range, so I have no doubts about the numbers that were produced. Every procedure was followed that we would follow for any sample. There was nothing different about this sample.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I have no more questions for you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Just a couple of questions please. You explained to us that the sample has to be frozen to maintain its integrity?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: If it's not frozen, does that undermine -- or does the sample deteriorate or is there a risk of the sample deteriorating?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it very much depends on the time window of that. So we have procedures in the documentation that -- we've said about the SOPs -- that would say with what window we would accept a sample if it had arrived, say, in the post. But obviously this arrived frozen. But if it had come in the post and we didn't have any sort of questionable time window about how long that sample had been defrosted for --
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. If it had arrived unfrozen, what's the time window that you look at for a sample like this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, it very much depends on the assay. So depending on what analyte, because some are more stable than others, but easily this insulin and C-peptide, because we have added them on -- and by that I mean if suddenly somebody had said, I've got a reason to request it, we would add it on to a sample, so we would accept it within 12 to 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Okay. If it hasn't been frozen in the right way, is there a risk of that affecting the accuracy of results?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it hasn't then, there is a risk but obviously with this we knew the time window from the time of the sample being taken to when we'd received it was within 24 hours anyway, even though it arrived frozen.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: The sample was taken at 17.56 on the 5th, wasn't it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- which is about 22 hours before you received it?

blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Organisation On Standardisation, that would be within their acceptable range for potential discrepancies.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Whichever is the more accurate, what we have here is an unacceptably low level; is that the essence of it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The essence of it is, whether it's 1.3 or 1.9, it is very low.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I just want to check my reference before I ask you the next question. You refer in your report, in the same paragraph that we've just dealt with, to the results that were obtained by Dr Milan's laboratory at the Royal Liverpool University Hospital. If Mr Murphy could put that on the screen, please. It's J26407, I think.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is what Dr Milan spoke of about an hour ago or so. What do we see there, please, professor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So we've got the sample, along with its timestamp of collection, at 17.56 hours on 5 April (sic). It's a serum sample. And depicted below the dashed line are the results of the analysis undertaken and verified and released on 6 August at 16.15 hours. They show the measurement of C-peptide, which is quoted there at less than 169. The units aren't stated but we know that that is in picomoles per litre.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We know, we've heard evidence of the fact that they don't -- the machine cannot detect anything less than 169. It could be between zero and 169.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's in evidence now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: You also have the insulin concentrations measured at the same time, 671 milliunits per litre and then in the -- in molar terms, that is the SI units, 4,657 picomoles per litre.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Dr Milan told us that comparing the 4,657 figure for insulin with the C-peptide figure in the same units, the Cpeptide figure should be anything between 5 and 10 times the size of the insulin figure; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I certainly said that in my documentation. I'm not entirely sure I heard her say that, but I may have missed it.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: She did say it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Fine. She is correct as well.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: You're both correct.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: We're both correct.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Very good. Can we deal next with your page 5, professor, and with the dangers of very low insulin.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you explain to the jury the effect of a depressed level of insulin -- sorry, I said the dangers of very low insulin, what I meant to say was the dangers of very low blood sugar. Could you tell then jury what are the dangers of very low blood sugar, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The brain is reliant on a constant supply of glucose for function, and it does not store any glucose in reserve to any significant degree. It has some -- it can store glucose as glycogen, but that will only last 20 minutes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: After that, there is no other energy available for functioning of the brain.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Now, fortunately, there is a slight way out of this problem and that is during hypoglycaemia, you can generate ketones and they're the breakdown products from fat. So you can break down fat as a source of energy and the brain will utilise the ketone bodies that are from that breakdown of fat as a substitute for the glucose that's missing. That's absolutely brilliant, it serves all of us very well indeed, and babies in particular, apart from one situation.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That is if your low blood glucose, hypoglycaemia, is caused by an excess of insulin. Insulin will do two things. The first thing it will do is it will reduce blood glucose, as we've been talking about already. So you've lost your glucose, you have lost that source of energy. Can you fall back on ketone bodies? The answer is no. So the second problem with a high amount of insulin is that it will switch off ketone body formation. So in the situation of hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia -- I apologise for the terminologies but that's what we're talking about, lots of insulin producing a low blood glucose -- the brain is now in a very, very susceptible state to incurring damage.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That damage depends a little bit on the duration of hypoglycaemia and also the depth of the hypoglycaemia.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Now, initially, if you go down to a blood glucose of 2.6 or 3, then you'll have mild confusion and if you are involved in any cognitive process, such as reading and writing, then there will be a deterioration in that.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: But as we progress further down in terms of the blood glucose delivered to the brain, and that's not much, then it can lead on to seizures, death of brain cells, coma and, on occasions, death.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So thus far, we have your opinion that the insulin in [Baby F]'s system was exogenous. You've just told us about the dangers -- well, you've told us also that the depression in blood sugar coincided with the administration of fluids and you've told us of the potential consequences of administering exogenous insulin to anybody and, in particular, to a baby.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I'd like to move on to, if we may, professor, is page 8 of your report, the means by which, in your opinion, the evidence suggests that this insulin was administered to [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So it may be of some assistance to the jury to have one eye at least on the chart that you have -- the table that you have produced for us. Can you talk us through your conclusions so far as how it was this insulin was administered to [Baby F]? And can we start, please, with your understanding of the type of insulin that was available at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The insulin in use, and has been in use for the last 20/25 years or so, possibly more, is synthetic insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We do not have stocks of what were the animal insulins, that's the pig and cow insulins, they would not be held as regular stocks, either on wards or in the hospital pharmacy, they would have to be requested in their own right. So we're talking about the synthetic human insulins.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: These split into two groupings. One is the short-acting insulins, which, as their name suggests, act quite quickly within 30 minutes, 60 minutes, if given by the under-the-skin injection route, and tend to last, in terms of their duration of action, for something between 4 and 6 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: There are two types. One is where the chemists have created an insulin that looks identical to human insulin, and that's the commonest ward stock, known as Actrapid. There are other insulins that you may hear about, such as NovoRapid Aspart or Humalog, and these are synthetic, but they have a modification made to one of the amino acids, one of the building blocks of the insulin molecule, to alter their onset of action.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We don't tend to use those as ward stock for any intravenous infusions if we need them. So on the ward, the most likely insulin available for use in any situation would be Actrapid insulin, synthetic human insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I would like to just show you --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, before we do that, you said there are two groupings, a short-acting one, and then did you run on to describe the second one?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I did not, my Lord. Thank you for picking me up on that.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The other type is long-acting insulins, which currently are modified in a way to prolong the duration of action up to 12 or 24 hours. They're predominantly given by the subcutaneous, under the skin, route.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I have never seen any information on them being given intravenously.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You're familiar with these substances from your working life, I've assumed. Can I produce to you a vial of Actrapid insulin that was obtained from the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: (Handed)
Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'd quite like to hand it round the jury in a moment, please, my Lord. That on its face, I think, appears to be a 10ml bottle; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It's 100 units in 1ml and these are the standard 10ml vials.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And just so the jury can have this in mind when they look at it, normally the bottle would be capped with what is within the bag as an orange -- yellowy-orange cap; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. It's in the bag itself, it's not attached.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The reason it's been removed is because if one looks under the cap, one sees in effect a self-sealing cap; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It's a latex bung, essentially.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And if a medical professional wanting to extract -- how would a medical professional extract insulin from that bottle?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You would need a needle and syringe, and if you're using it therapeutically you would use an insulin -- a syringe graded to allow for an accurate dose, the drawing up of the insulin, because this is quite concentrated, this is 100 units per ml and we would probably -- we would be talking perhaps in ourselves of perhaps using no more than about 2 or 3 units given subcutaneously, or 5 units perhaps.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So you'd need a very accurate insulin syringe to -- if you wished to dose therapeutically. Then you would have to add a needle to that, put the needle through the resealable latex bung, draw up the desired amount, and withdraw the needle and syringe.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: When you say using it therapeutically, do you mean using it legitimately for legitimate treatment?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, a prescribed insulin dose.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. And that would have to be measured very, very carefully?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It would.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I wonder whether the jury could see the bottle, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I wonder if I could take a look first, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)

Professor, what I'm going to do now, if I may, is deal with how this exogenous insulin was administered and then I will ask you ultimately how much of this went into the liquid that was being administered, so the jury know where I'm going.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Before I do that, can I formally exhibit this bottle and packaging, my Lord, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm told I didn't make it entirely clear through you, professor. The needle attached to the syringe goes through the latex bung, and when it's withdrawn the bottle self-seals in effect; is that the position?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We can see for ourselves how much liquid is in there and we'll turn in due course to how much was removed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you consider, in the light of the evidence that was available, how insulin was administered to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did. I think probably what we should say right at the outset is that it is not possible to give insulin by mouth, by the oral route, because it's a large molecule, so it can't be absorbed very easily. And the second thing is that it is -because it's a protein, it would be broken down or damaged by the acid in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So we're not talking about any form of oral administration or administration through a nasogastric tube, for example. We are talking about the administration of insulin either by the intravenous route or by subcutaneous administration, under the skin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'll deal with the subcutaneous route, if I may, first of all. In my report, and also in one of the exhibits I provided, I give the time course of insulin.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: That's figure 2, my Lord, in my report. But the point about the subcutaneous route is that with a duration of action of 4 to 6 hours, and over the period that we've documented of some 17 hours of hypoglycaemia, that would require multiple subcutaneous injections, as I say roughly every 4 to 6 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And the first one would have been at what time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: To get that effect you'd probably have to do that almost at the same time as you set up the total parenteral nutrition bag. The argument against that is there would be quite few injections and also it would be then difficult to start to explain why you had such a quick return towards normal blood glucose, particularly as you can see in the chart that was sent round that when the TPN, the total parenteral nutrition, stopped at 18.55, we almost had an almost instantaneous rise to 2.5. But by 21.17 hours we had achieved normoglycaemia, whereas if we had been relying on subcutaneous injections, we wouldn't have seen such a rapid response in terms of the blood glucose, which would imply that probably an intravenous route is the most likely explanation.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So for that reason, dealing with the intravenous route as being, in your opinion, the route by which this insulin was administered, how was it done?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So intravenously there's two ways of doing it. The first would be to give bolus injections of insulin. And we know. When we do this in certain tests that we do in endocrinology. That hypoglycaemia will occur 20 to 30 minutes after the bolus injection. If you don't do anything else, the blood glucose will then start to rise back up again and be normal some 60 to 90 minutes after the bolus injection. So what you would need to do in this situation to maintain hypoglycaemia over such a protracted period of time is that you'd have to undertake multiple intravenous injections roughly every 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Might I continue, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Please do, yes. Don't worry about watching my pen because I'm taking notes, but I'm listening as well. Just carry on. If I ask you to pause -- if I need you to pause, I'll ask you to pause.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Otherwise you carry on. You're speaking slowly and clearly and we're all picking this up, I'm sure.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So the second way of administering insulin intravenously is through an infusion. I think that this is probably the most likely way of achieving the blood glucose effects that we've observed. It would be a continuous infusion, using the bags of fluid that were available.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: It would fit nicely with the time course of events when the fluids were discontinued for re-siting the cannula at 10.00 hours on 5 August and would also be consistent with the events or measurements that took place after the total parenteral nutrition was stopped at 18.55 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Those two points, but particularly the 18.55 hours one, fit from calculations I undertook. Assuming that the insulin was present in a steady state, at discontinuation of the TPN, for example at 18.55, that would be consistent with the disappearance of insulin from the circulation.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So if you had a concentration of 4,657 picomoles per litre at 18.55, when your total parenteral nutrition is switched off, then 32 minutes later -- sorry about the numbers because that's because of the half-life of insulin, which is 4 minutes -- 32 minutes later there would only be 18 picomoles per litre, which is a normal fasting plasma insulin concentration. So that we could be sure that by the time we got to 19.30 hours, after the discontinuation of the infusions at 18.55, there would be almost no insulin in the circulation -- perhaps I should qualify that: there would be no exogenous insulin present in the circulation by 19.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And because of the way in which insulin is removed so quickly from the circulation, it also means that the effect of the insulin on the cells to produce hypoglycaemia would be terminated fairly rapidly after that, so the rise of the blood glucose to 4.1 at 21.17 hours is entirely consistent with that — with the pharmacology.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Did you calculate from the blood sugar results the rate at which insulin was being -- exogenous insulin was being administered to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did, and to maintain a steady state insulin concentration of 4,657 picomoles per litre, we would need an insulin infusion rate of approximately 1.18 or 1.2 units per hour. And from that, we could add on some slight amounts to deal with adhesiveness of insulin to plastic in the infusion bags or in the giving sets, the cannulas, but that's only going to be about 10% or 15%.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: If we say 1.2 units per hour would be the infusion rate you would need to deliver to get a plasma insulin concentration of 4,657 picomoles per litre then it's going to be in the region of about 1.2 milliunits -- units per hour.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that from your -- 1.2 units per hour is what he was receiving from your calculations.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I'd like to do is just look at J3151, please, which is the prescription of insulin to [Baby F] between 03.40 and 06.20 hours on 31 July. So comparing what he was given as treatment to what he was receiving on 5 August.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you look on the screen, professor, you see there under the "dose" row, the prescription for insulin, which lasted 5 hours and 40 minutes, was of 0.05 units/kg/hour. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. So that would be -- I can't do this in my head, so... So that's 0.07 units per hour, given he was 1.45 kilograms at that stage.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So in general terms, 1.2 is about 18 times or so the prescribed amount, give or take?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Give or take, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Well, 20 times would be 1.4, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Seventeen times, give or take.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I should point out, my Lord, that the infusion rates that you see on that chart are totally appropriate and exactly what we would use in standard care.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. So what we see on the screen now?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So that idea of 0.05 units per kilogram body weight per -- is the sort of number we would be going for.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So that's the appropriate therapeutic dose?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, to maintain a normal blood glucose.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: I'll come to in a moment the change in the bag, but just so that the jury know I'm going to deal with that point.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So having worked out how much [Baby F] was receiving, did that enable you to calculate the amount of insulin that must have been put into the TPN bag from which he was being treated?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I mean, that is -- it has been possible to do that. I came out for a -- for a bag lasting 24 hours, that would be about 28 units. Then I adjusted a little bit for the adhesiveness of insulin to plastic and allowed myself another 10 or 15%, which I think came out at then approximately 30 units. That would be the sort of amount that might be added.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: For a two-day bag, we have heard these bags are designed to run for 2 days --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, then I would double that to 60.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So 60. In terms of quantity, so that's units, we've heard that 10ml is 1,000 units. How much liquid needs to go into the bag to equate to the 60-odd units which was the concentration of the fluid being administered to [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you'd need 0.6ml.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So just over one half of 1 millilitre of liquid needs to be added to the TPN bag to deliver the rate of insulin that you have calculated [Baby F] was receiving?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: We've seen for ourselves what Actrapid insulin looks like. It's a clear fluid. Going into a bag of TPN, would it be visible to the naked eye?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, not at all, and I'd say clearly with those volumes you wouldn't notice a change in the shape or size of the bag.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Drawing a line across your table as to when the fluids were stopped, we have heard evidence that a stock bag was taken and used once the long line was re-sited.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just so that you understand the evidence, the initial bag hung just after midnight was a bespoke bag in the name of [Baby F]. And the evidence suggests that once the line was re-sited, to maintain the sterility of the process, a stock bag was taken.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Looking at the readings on your table, would it follow that the stock bag must have been contaminated as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it looks -- yes, it would imply that, yes, if that was the sequence of events.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Yes. And if that was the case, looking at the blood glucose measurements, would it also follow that the stock bag was contaminated to more or less the same degree as the bespoke bag?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that is not an unreasonable comment to make. We know that there is a reasonable dose response curve between insulin dose and effect. And with the exception of the 2.9 millimoles per litre that we had our attention drawn to at 05.00 hours, the glucose concentrations are not much different in the period of time from the 01.54 hours through to 10.00 hours when things were changed compared to that period of time from 12.00 hours through to the last measurement, which was undertaken at 18.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: So I think it's probably reasonable to say that they are -- the contents are probably about the same.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: The level of contamination is?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, yes.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: And thus did you conclude that the explanation for [Baby F]'s clinical presentation from just after midnight on 5 August to the early evening of the same day was explicable, and only reasonably explicable, by the fact that the fluid he was receiving had been contaminated with insulin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Thank you. It may be that there are some further questions for you, professor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Professor Hindmarsh, could I just ask you a couple of questions about insulin in general before I go to some of the detail you have given us.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If a quantity of insulin in the form of Actrapid was introduced into a clear solution, would that be visible or would it not be visible?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It would not be visible.
blocks.speaker: HINDMARSH

blocks.text: Does insulin, and I'm thinking about the form of Actrapid at the moment, have quite a distinctive smell if it's spilt or exposed to the air?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It does, because of the preservatives that are within it, which is -- it is usually the cresol component that gives it the distinctive smell.

blocks.text: Are you able to read the next line to us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Soft continuous murmur."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: What does that mean, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a whooshing sound that you get in the heart that is very common in premature babies. The most common cause is just what we call an innocent murmur, which changes as they get older. It is to do with increased blood flow through different parts of the heart. It can mean there's a hole in the heart or it can mean there's a little tube that's meant to close when you're born that hasn't, which if it's continuous it tends to be, but in most cases of one of those the close by themselves spontaneously over time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But what I have then written is "femorals ++" which is the femoral pulses. If there's a problem with this little tube that stays open the pulses are really, really strong and quite different to what you'd expect so if I thought that that was significant I would have written what we call "bounding" or "cannonball" pulses, which I have not written. And then I have put "fontanelle soft", which is again the soft spot on the skull.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The plan, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The plan I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Re-screen and second line antibiotics."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So screening is a term we use when we look for infection. So what that entails is taking bloods to look for infection, putting in a cannula and giving antibiotics. He was already on antibiotics and so if you are worried at all about any possibility of infection when you're on antibiotics, you change to a different antibiotic, so second line antibiotics, which were -- cefotaxime and teicoplanin were the ones we would go for next.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that was based on the fact that he was vomiting more and concerns around that heart rate being a bit high as well as concerns for the fact that his brother had, sadly, passed away the evening before.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I was about to ask you on what basis did you reach that plan, but you have told us it's really the first two entries on your note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We can go next, please, to note 177. Same shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: About an hour later, 2.30. More familiar handwriting this time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's mine, my atrocious handwriting, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Could you take us through the entry you have made on that occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have put "ATSP", which is "asked to see patient", so that is what we put if the nurses ask us to see them, regarding his tachycardia, which was 200 to 210 beats per minute as well as having large milky aspirates, so the milk coming up through the tube, and for --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, does it say aspirate or aspirates?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Aspirate, sorry. With -- and being quieter than normal -- sorry, quieter than usual. His heart rate on the monitor showed a rate of 200 to 210 beats with what we call narrow complexes. So if you look at an ECG normally what you have is a small bump, a big tall inverse V shape and then another small little bump.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: A narrow complex is what it should be, there should be quite a big -- a spike that's quite rapidly up and down with a very narrow spike.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: If it's abnormal, it can either be that you have lots and lots of those narrow spikes or you can have problems with a different part of your heart which are wide spikes, and they look quite different.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So what I was initially thinking at this point is that these narrow -- so what I'm looking at there is the narrow suggests this is either normal or. Something which I'm sure you'll ask me about, the SVT.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Unable to clearly see P waves due to size of complexes."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So the P wave is the little bump that you get before you get this V -- inverse V shape. If that's there, it's normal. If it's not there, it suggests something called a supraventricular tachycardia or SVT. If it happened to an adult your heart rate normally is slower, so even if it's going faster you'd be able to work it out. Whereas with babies when it's that fast they're so close together that you can't actually see these little -very clearly on the monitor.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just pausing there then, this is something you're seeing in real time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, this is on the monitors at this point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay. What was it, it might be obvious from your answer, that was troubling you most about what you could see at this stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So with infection, heart rates can go a bit quickly.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Stress and pain can make their heart rates go quicker.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But more often than not, they're sitting around 180, 190. It's rare for them to go to 200 and stay around the 200, 200-plus mark. So that's my main concern: why is this fast and staying fast. If it was pain, if it was when I did a cannula, it might go up to 200 for a few seconds or a minute and come back down, but this being quite persistent over the hour or so from what I remember and from looking through the notes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It moves on to septic screen.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "So septic screen undertaken. Bloods sent for FBC [full blood count], CRP [C-reactive protein], U&Es (inaudible) bilirubin and lactate."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And then I have also sent a sample for blood culture and I have also sent that for a blood gas as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The initial -- are these the abbreviations --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: These are the abbreviations at the end.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- at the end of the sentence?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then on the blood gas which is the test that we do to look at the amount of acid in the blood, to suggest whether there's infection or to suggest if there's any problems with getting oxygen around the body, it also shows us the blood sugar, or glucose, which was 0.8, which is very low.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Does the blood gas indicate any other difficulties from recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not from recollection, no.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You've examined him again. On examination, I think we have O/E.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I have put he handles well, so he's acting like a baby would act normally. He's pink, so's getting blood supply around his body and is well-perfused and his cap refill time -so when you push on his chest for 5 seconds and take it off -is less than 2 seconds, which is normal as well, so I am happy with everything at that point.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: His heart sounds were normal, still has this murmur, but very quiet, his heart rate was still 200, and he still have good pulses which was reassuring. His chest was still clear, his abdomen was still soft and non-tender with good bowel sounds and no masses and his --
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I am just going to ask to you pause there. We've moved on, but the word systolic appears in your earlier entry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry. In your heart, you have two different sounds.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have your sounds where things are beating, so the top part of your heart beats and then it retracts so you have boom-boom.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The systolic sounds is that first sound so a systolic murmur would kind of be a boom-shhhh sound in between.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There are different types. A continuous one would literally just be a whoosh-whoosh-whoosh sound in between the two different beats of the heart that you hear, the two different noises.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So systolic murmurs are a lot more quiet and those tend to be the ones that are either innocent or some holes in the heart or this duct, the PDA which is this little extra tube, so those tend to fit with those, and are relatively common, particularly in a stressed baby as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Moving on, AF again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So AF is the anterior fontanelle, the soft spot, which was normotensive, so as it should be normally.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right. And if we move down the page again, please, you have identified things that were troubling you; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Number 1 was hypoglycaemia, so low blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Number 2 was the tachycardia, the fast heart rate, where I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "[Query] SVT [the supraventricular tachycardia] or [query] second to sepsis."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, we heard a little bit about SVT from Dr Gibbs, but just in a nutshell, please remind us what SVT is.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So SVT or supraventricular tachycardia -- essentially you have got the pacemaker of the heart, which is in the top chambers of the right, that sends a message to the rest of your heart to beat. Sometimes what happens is either there's a problem with feedback, and it keeps on firing, or somewhere else nearby fires that messages (sic). So what happens is rather than having a nice regular beat, it fires so many messages that your heart just keeps on beating faster and faster and faster. We see that not too uncommonly and that tends to be -- with heart rates in the 200s to 300s that we tend to suspect that.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is the question mark a query?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So you query SVT?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Query SVT.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you also query --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Query] second to sepsis."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So they were the two things running through your mind at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You then set out a plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "2ml per kg dextrose bolus."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So the dextrose being a different type of sugar that will help bring the sugar level up. I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "10ml per kilogram of 0.9% saline [so salt water] bolus."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So -- because if the heart rate's going faster we think, is he dehydrated, is there extra stress on his body, is this infection that is driving it, so giving some fluids can help reduce some of that pressure on the heart and help to reduce it. I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Started on second line antibiotics."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The cefotaxime and teicoplanin. He had a long line in place so the other thing we look for is if there's infection in the line, and if there's infection in the line you'd start a different type of antibiotic, which is teicoplanin. That's one that you use especially when you're looking for that. So that was why that choice was.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then a 12-lead ECG. So an ECG looks at those little squiggles of the heart, a 12-lead looks at it from different angles and there's a much more sophisticated way of picking up problems with the heart better than the monitor, so we asked for one of those as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Then "consider adenosine". Adenosine is a medication which will slow the heart down -- very rapidly will bring it down. It will bring it down incredibly low and can cause problems in itself, it can go too low and potentially stop the heart. So we only use that if we're really convinced this is an SVT, hence why it wasn't something we jumped for.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And finally, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was it, sorry. "Consider adenosine", that was the last one.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Sorry, okay. And we can see your signature there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Next tile, please. A third entry on your behalf, Dr Harkness, at 187. Same handwriting, so this is you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It's 3.30 now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So another hour passes. Is that the 12-lead ECG you're telling us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That shows the heart rate of 204. It shows narrow complexes -- so like I'd said, these very narrow inverse V shapes, and I still couldn't see these P waves, these little lumps that come before this V shape. What 25 millimetres per second or 50 millimetres per second is -- you can slow down how fast the paper moves through the machine. So if you halve the speed it's going through it makes everything look broader and makes it easier to try and see these little bumps that are called the P waves. And I still at that couldn't see it.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: QTC is a corrected -- I've completely forgotten what I'm doing now -- is the corrected QT, which is -- your Q wave is part of the large V that comes up and comes down, and your T wave is the bump that comes afterwards which is when the electricity goes back to where it should be. And we measure that time and if that's long that can make you go into these SVTs essentially.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So 0.44/0.45, tends to be around the upper limit of where we would say -- 0.44 is normally the figure we'd say, so around that upper limit.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So having had the results of that ECG, you then discuss, do you, with Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And can you tell us what the outcome of that discussion was, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So Dr Gibbs felt this was unlikely SVT as the rate would likely be closer to 300 rather than 200. So like I said before, when the baby's heart rate goes faster anyway, you expect it to be faster, and 250 to 300 tends to be more of what we'd see with SVT rather than just over the 200 mark. So his
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: suggestion was to repeat the fluid bolus of another 10ml per kilogram of saline and continue to monitor and only to give the adenosine, this medicine that slows the heart, if the heart rate goes up to around the 300 point.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: That's because of the risks that you described to us a moment or two ago?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Scroll down again, please. Some more results there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So what I put there is "full blood count" at the top.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: There's "HB", which is the red blood cells of 140, which is normal. White cells, normal range. And platelets, normal range. The only thing that was slightly abnormal was the creatine, which is there as "creat" of 94.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You'd normally expect that to be in the 30s/40s, and 94 would suggest he's possibly a little bit dehydrated.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I've put "awaiting calcium". Calcium is something that can cause -- if it's abnormal can cause irregularities in the way that the heart beats, essentially. So my impression from that point was: is this dehydration that's making his heart go fast because he needs more fluid? Is this sepsis? But we were happy that the heart rate wasn't fast enough for this to be an SVT, so I've then put "unlikely SVT". So the plan at that point otherwise was to continue to monitor his sugars. I've not mentioned his sugars in that note there, but they were on the -- recorded on the charts.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Right, okay. Just dealing with sugar, can we go next, please, Mr Murphy, to tile 191, and the form behind it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Intravenous and subcutaneous infusion prescription chart. Are you familiar with that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Can I ask you please to look initially -- if we go please to the entry on 5 August timed at 3.50. 3.50 am.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to highlight it so we're sure it's the one we're talking about.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So there are a series of entries there in the early hours of 5 August. By your reaction, do you recognise the entry at 03.50?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So what I would have done at that point is because we were thinking of dehydration, if we want to give more fluids rather than giving TPN, which we were already on, we also then will add on 10% dextrose on top to give extra fluids and extra sugar as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's an infusion, that one, so that's a rate of 50ml per kilo per day, so we would have increased from whatever his daily amount was on TPN and then, because we needed more, it would have gone up on the sugar instead. So I don't know from there how much he was on, but that would be in addition as well as having the boluses either side.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Forgive me, but why the extra sugar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the sugar in that was more because that's the fluids we always use regardless -- will be 10% dextrose. The dextrose, 3ml of which -- there are several, those were a bolus, so those are given over a couple of minutes and those are to correct the sugar as soon as possible, whereas the infusion is there as additional. It's primarily there to give additional water and hydrate as well as giving the sugar as well. So that one's more for his hydration as opposed to sugar at that point in time, but he'd had multiple sugar boluses as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is that your signature beneath the "prescribed by" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We can see your signature on a number of entries; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Just going down the page to the 4.20. I think you were just telling us about a bolus to boost the sugar levels.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we go to that, please? Is that another one of your prescriptions?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And for the reason that you have just set out for us.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: far as you recall, did any of these measures to boost the sugar have an effect on [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I'd need to look at the exact chart. I think all of them had an effect to bring it close to the regular range that we wanted, but they kept drifting up and down, which is why we needed to keep giving them.
